summary: Extends aggregate RSVP reservations, which reserve resources in a Diffserv network for a given per-hop behavior between two points. RFC 3175 defined the basic idea. This document generalizes it to cases where multiple sources or destinations share the aggregate reservation. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Instead of booking a lane for each car, you book one big lane for a whole group. This lets the group have many starting points or many stopping points.

subtitle: Lets several aggregate RSVP reservations share the same endpoints and traffic class, for example one per preemption priority.

tldr.problem: The aggregate RSVP reservations of RFC 3175 allow only one reservation per source address, destination address and PHB (or set of PHBs). Some deployments need several, such as one per preemption priority.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4860 defines a generic aggregate SESSION object that adds a Virtual Destination Port and an Extended Virtual Destination Port, and identifies the PHB by PHB-ID rather than DSCP. A new SESSION-OF-INTEREST object tells the Aggregator which session to use.
tldr.outcome: Many generic aggregate reservations can exist between the same pair of addresses for the same PHB. They can aggregate end-to-end reservations or be used directly by end-systems or by configuration.

today: RFC 4860 is a Proposed Standard from May 2007. The unit metadata shows nothing that obsoletes or updates it, and it builds on RFC 3175.

sections.title: The Limit of One Aggregate per PHB
sections.content:
RFC 3175 defines aggregate RSVP reservations: resources reserved in a Diffserv network for a flow identified by source address, destination address and Diffserv Code Point (DSCP). Many end-to-end (E2E) reservations can be aggregated onto one of these as they cross a Diffserv cloud. The router where aggregation begins is the Aggregator and the one where it ends is the Deaggregator.

The catch is that between a given source and destination only a single aggregate reservation can exist for a given PHB (or set of PHBs). The RFC gives the example of E2E reservations with different preemption priorities that must cross the cloud using the same PHB. Separate aggregates for each priority let the aggregation region enforce those priorities, and in a resource shortage keep more of the higher-priority E2E reservations.

RFC 4860 solves this with a more flexible type, the generic aggregate reservation. It reuses RFC 3175 wherever it can and specifies only the differences.
sections.eli5: The old rule allowed just one big lane between two places for each kind of traffic. But sometimes you want two lanes for the same traffic, one with priority access.

sections.title: How Sessions Become More Specific
sections.content:
Two ideas are borrowed from other RSVP work. The Virtual Destination Port comes from RFC 2207, where it identifies sessions beyond the IP destination address. The Extended Tunnel ID of RFC 3209 is reused and renamed Extended Virtual Destination Port; it lets the Aggregator put its own address in the session to narrow it to one Aggregator and Deaggregator pair.

The PHB is identified by the PHB-ID of RFC 3140 instead of the DSCP. A PHB-ID states explicitly whether one PHB or a set is meant, and it works when a reservation spans Diffserv domains that use different DSCP values for the same PHB.

If the Extended Virtual Destination Port is all zeros, the session is common to several senders, so they share a reservation. If an Aggregator places its own address there, the reservation is limited to that Aggregator and Deaggregator pair.
sections.eli5: Each big lane gets a little extra name tag, so two lanes between the same places can be told apart. Putting your own name on the tag makes the lane yours alone; leaving it blank lets a group share it.

sections.title: The New RSVP Objects
sections.content:
RFC 4860 defines two new SESSION objects under class 1: GENERIC-AGGREGATE-IP4 (C-Type 17) and GENERIC-AGGREGATE-IP6 (C-Type 18). Each carries the destination address (of the receiver or Deaggregator), a Reserved byte, a Flags byte, the 16-bit PHB-ID, a 16-bit vDstPort and the Extended vDstPort. The extended field is 32 bits for IPv4 and 128 bits for IPv6. Reserved bits MUST be zero on transmit and are ignored on receipt.

It also defines a new class, SESSION-OF-INTEREST (class 132), with GENERIC-AGG-IP4-SOI (C-Type 1) and GENERIC-AGG-IP6-SOI (C-Type 2). These simply carry a copy of the generic aggregate SESSION of another reservation. A SESSION-OF-INTEREST object does not replace the SESSION object in a message.

All the new objects are optional for RSVP in general, but routers that support generic aggregate or aggregation over them MUST support the matching objects.
sections.eli5: The new objects are forms with a few extra boxes to fill in. One form names the lane, and another form lets one message point at a lane mentioned in a different message.

sections.title: Processing and Aggregation Procedures
sections.content:
For Path messages with a generic aggregate session, only the RFC 3175 aggregate sender template may be used. The PHB-ID, vDstPort and Extended vDstPort become part of the session state. The PHB-ID may be passed to traffic control, but the two port values are not, because they do not appear in the data packets. Routers classify data by DSCP only, using the DSCPs tied to the PHB-ID. If fine-grain classification is needed, the 3-tuple of destination address, source address and DSCP is used. Reservations that differ only in port values then cannot be told apart, so a router that polices them MUST set the policing rate to the sum of their reserved rates.

The Deaggregator asks for a new aggregate by sending an E2E PathErr with error code NEW-AGGREGATE-NEEDED. It MUST include a SESSION-OF-INTEREST object holding the generic aggregate session to use, so the DCLASS object is not needed. By choosing different port values per Aggregator, or the same values, it decides whether reservations are separate or shared. The Aggregator then MUST start sending aggregate Path messages for that session, and MUST copy a signaled preemption priority element into them if one was sent.

In the E2E Resv message the Deaggregator MUST include SESSION-OF-INTEREST to say which generic aggregate the E2E reservation maps onto. The Aggregator MUST NOT include it when sending the Resv upstream. When an aggregate is no longer needed the Deaggregator MUST send an aggregate ResvTear, and the Aggregator SHOULD answer with an aggregate PathTear unless policy says otherwise.

The RFC also recommends that Aggregator and Deaggregator use interface-independent addresses, such as a loopback address, when identifying themselves to each other, so an interface failure causes a reroute rather than a teardown. Generic aggregates may also be set up by end-systems such as PSTN gateways, or by static configuration between ingress and egress routers.
sections.eli5: The router at the far end asks the router at the near end to open a new lane and tells it the lane's name tag. Every later request for a car says which lane it rides in, and when the lane is no longer needed it is closed.

sections.title: Example: Voice with Two Preemption Priorities
sections.content:
The RFC's example has three Aggregator/Deaggregator routers (Agg-Deag-1, -2, -3) around an aggregation region, carrying voice E2E reservations that use the EF PHB. E2E reservations from Cloud-1 and Cloud-2 to Cloud-3 have preemption priority P1 or P2, and traffic is carried in GRE tunnels.

Four generic aggregates result. From Agg-Deag-1 to Agg-Deag-3 there are two, with vDstPort values V1 and V2 and preemption priorities P1 and P2. From Agg-Deag-2 to Agg-Deag-3 there are two more, with V3 and V4. All use PHB-ID EF, and the Extended vDstPort holds the source Aggregator's address. The vDstPort values are picked by Agg-Deag-3, and V3 and V4 could equal V1 and V2.
sections.eli5: Two neighbourhoods each book two lanes to the same stadium: a VIP lane and a regular lane. All four lanes carry the same kind of traffic but are kept apart by their tags.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RSVP Authentication from RFC 2747 and RFC 3097 may be used to protect message integrity hop by hop, including for E2E messages crossing the aggregation region, because the Aggregator and Deaggregator act as RSVP neighbors. Manual key distribution is the mandated base option. Using it where IP hops lie between RSVP neighbors is harder, since a Path message is sent before the next hop is known, so one approach is to share one key across all Aggregators and Deaggregators of a region. The RFC says automated key management for unicast flows across domains is not currently clear and leaves it out of scope.

RSVP Authentication gives no confidentiality; IPsec ESP may be used. It does not protect against traffic analysis either, and since an aggregate covers many users, snooping on it can reveal more. The RFC also warns that losing an aggregate to an aggressor leaves many E2E flows unreserved, and that malicious changes to the IP protocol number in Path messages could stop reservations. It RECOMMENDS supporting such changes only for RSVP Path, PathTear and ResvConf messages.
sections.eli5: Because one big lane serves many cars, a trick played on it hurts many people at once. So the lane's messages should be signed, and only the few messages that really need changing should be changeable.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned C-Types 17 (GENERIC-AGGREGATE-IP4) and 18 (GENERIC-AGGREGATE-IP6) under the existing SESSION class, number 1 from RFC 2205. It also assigned the new class number 132 for SESSION-OF-INTEREST, with C-Types 1 and 2 for the IPv4 and IPv6 forms. These allocations follow the procedures for modifying RSVP in RFC 3936.
sections.eli5: The official number list was updated so everyone uses the same numbers for the new forms.

fields.name: IPv4 DestAddress
fields.desc: Address of the receiver or Deaggregator.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on transmit, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Same as the IPv4/UDP SESSION Flags.

fields.name: PHB-ID
fields.desc: Identifies the PHB or set of PHBs.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on transmit, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: vDstPort
fields.desc: Virtual Destination Port, constant for the reservation's life.

fields.name: Extended vDstPort
fields.desc: Aggregator address to narrow scope, or all zeros to share.
